Media Give The Drug Czar Free Ride On Prohibitionist Propaganda
Against Medical Marijuana Initiatives -- 2 Articles

Any report that does not address the fact that seriously ill, dying and disabled people are being arrested and prosecuted for using marijuana is complicit in this cruelty. These two articles studiously ignore reality.)

October 28, 1998

(Adds comment from pro-marijuana lobbyists, paras 9-11)

By Mahmoud Kassem

WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Federal anti-drug officials on Tuesday urged voters to reject initiatives to legalize the medicinal use of marijuana that are on the Nov. 3 ballot in four states and the District of Columbia.

"Smoked marijuana has not been tested (by the government)," Dr. Don Vereen, deputy director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy told a news conference.

(Marijuananews note: Of course, this is untrue. The government has been giving eight Americans 300 joints per month under a so-called Investigative New Drug program for years. These people are all deriving the benefits which they were seeking from the marijuana and none of them are showing any adverse side-effects. If the government does not know about this they must want not to know. Do these reporters know this? Do they want to know?)

"We must keep an open mind about drugs with medical purposes, (but) before you vote, ask yourself: ‘What other medicines do you smoke?’
See

Smoked marijuana damages the brain, heart, lungs and immune system."

The ballot initiatives in Alaska, Nevada, Oregon, Washington state and Washington, D.C. seek to allow doctors to recommend the smoking of marijuana for AIDS, cancer and terminally ill patients.

Voters in California and Arizona approved measures in recent years to legalize marijuana for medical uses, but legal challenges and other controversies in both states have prevented full implementation.

Federal anti-drug officials believe the initiatives will undermine the legitimate medical use of cannabis.

(Marijuananews note: Oh, do they really "believe" that? This is a new one. If the synthetic is as effective as the whole plant how will that happen? Does this mean that people might want to use marijuana because it costs less and works better? If not then what does that mean?)

They also fear that medicinal marijuana initiatives will undermine their drug prevention programs.

"These marijuana referenda come at a time when we can’t afford to send the wrong message to our children about smoking marijuana,"

"Let’s have none of this malarkey (nonsense) on marijuana smoking by cunning groups working to legalize drugs. American medicine is the best in the world for pain management," he said.
See
Study Faults Pain Treatment In Cancer Patients; "Most doctors are not well trained to manage pain." Just Our Lives

(Marijuananews note: Notice that the quotes from NORML are inserted immediately after the allegation about "cunning groups.")

The NORML Foundation, a nonprofit lobby working to end marijuana prohibition, said it has compiled a database of over 40 medical organizations that support medical marijuana research or therapeutic use.

"Over the past several years, the medical community has resoundingly spoken in favor of allowing certain patients legal access to medical marijuana," said Allen Pierre, executive director of The NORML foundation.

"It remains politicians in Washington and law enforcement officials, not doctors and nurses, who continue to support policies prohibiting the use of marijuana as a legal medicine," he added.

The National Academy of Science’s Institute of Medicine is scheduled to complete its report for the government on "medical marijuana" in January.

(Marijuananews note: Notice the "quotation marks" around medical marijuana. There is no similar use of them in the article.)

October 27, 1998

From Chicago Tribune
Knight Ridder/Tribune Information Services
tribletter@aol.com
http://www.chicagotribune.com/

By Naftali Bendavid (KRT)

(Marijuananews note: This is really bad journalism. While it does present the "anecdotal" evidence about medical marijuana, from the headline down it is written from the prohibitionist perspective and does not begin to reflect the reality of scientific support for medical marijuana.)

(Marijuananews note: The headline is the premise for the prohibitionist allegation that medical marijuana is a "Trojan Horse" – "red herring" – "scam" – "to legalize all drugs.")

WASHINGTON—Renee Emry walked into the office of Rep. Bill McCollum last month and did something rarely seen in a congressional suite: She lit up a marijuana cigarette.

Emry, 38, suffers from multiple sclerosis, and she wanted to urge McCollum, R-Fla., to support the legalization of marijuana as medicine for patients like herself.
See

"I find that when I medicate appropriately, it calms my nerves, so I fired up a fatty,"said Emry, who came here from Ann Arbor, Mich., on behalf of a group called the Marijuana Policy Project. "It’s not like I was trying to be rude, crude and totally uncalled for. I was there to educate the man."

Whisked away by Capitol police, Emry faces trial on a drug charge in December.

Not so easily ushered away is the issue itself. Medical marijuana initiatives may be the first proposals for relaxing the drug laws that have gained significant support since the war on drugs began in earnest in the early 1980s.

Voters in California and Arizona approved medical marijuana initiatives two years ago. Five more Western states, plus the District of Columbia, will vote on similar proposals next Tuesday, and polls released by supporters this week suggest they will win handily.
(Marijuananews note: Notice that there is nothing here about the Congress blocking the D.C. vote.)
See A Great Press Release From D.C. Medical Marijuana Supporters

While those polls may be suspect, (Marijuananews note: This is the first time that I have ever seen a journalist question the validity of poll numbers. Certainly, they never question the prohibitionist’s polls that purport to show the levels of marijuana use among teens.) the public does face a real prospect of waking up after election day to find that medical marijuana is legal, at least in theory, in seven states that cover about one-fifth of the population.

Police, prosecutors and federal officials are beside themselves with frustration.

"This is a way to legally introduce people to possibly a lifetime of drug abuse," said John Justice, a South Carolina prosecutor who heads the National District Attorneys Association. "The drug problem from stem to stern in this country is tremendous, and I knew a judge who used to call marijuana‘the kindergarten of the drug industry.""

The proposals’ supporters hope they are establishing a beachhead, and that eventually marijuana will be legally available from doctors nationwide.

(Marijuananews note: Excuse me again, but it could be both. Many dangerous drugs are medically available. The public knows this.)
See

"Legally there is little significance if these things pass, but politically there is a lot of significance," said Eric Sterling, president of the Criminal Justice Policy Foundation. "Members of Congress might start to re-evaluate their position."

It is not entirely an accident that medical marijuana is catching on now. A group called Americans for Medical Rights, headquartered in Santa Monica, Calif., is pushing the crusade with small staffs in several states.

AMR is bankrolled by three millionaires:

The campaign is airing commercials that stress the theme of compassion. An Oregon television spot, for example, shows an avuncular doctor bemoaning his inability to help patients suffering with chemotherapy. "Please, let us treat you with every medicine that can help," Dr. Rick Bayer begs viewers.

Public officials and anti-drug activists are furious at this campaign. But there is little organized opposition or advertising on the other side, and that is one reason supporters are confident of victory.

(Marijuananews note: I know for a fact that the reporter was told about government funding of the opposition, but he chose to ignore it.)

Rep. McCollum, who pushed through a congressional resolution against medical marijuana, claimed the drug can actually hurt patients by weakening their immune systems. It is misleading for the initiatives to suggest that marijuana would be available at the corner drugstore, McCollum added, when in fact it would remain illegal to sell it even if the initiatives pass.

"It is always phrased as though the doctor is going to provide a prescription," McCollum said. "In reality, there is no prescription. The doctor gives you a chit and you can go down the street and buy it from anyone."

(Marijuananews note: Yes, but it would be legal under state law to possess it and the patient would not be subject to arrest by local law enforcement. The DEA is hardly equipped to go after every medical marijuana user. That is the whole point from the patient perspective.)

Opponents see a sinister agenda, the legalization of all drugs, hiding behind the mask of compassion.

"They are taking the case to the voters in the most obnoxious and irresponsible way, crafting television commercials that appeal to compassion for the terminally ill," said Sue Rusche, executive director of the anti-drug group National Families in Action. "Who doesn’t have compassion for the terminally ill?" (Marijuananews note: Who indeed?)
See

Behind the social question—is this just a way for old hippies to push through drug legalization? -- is a medical one: Does marijuana really have therapeutic value?
(Marijuananews note: He has just said that the principle support has come from three businessmen. He says nothing about the D.C. initiative that grew out of the AIDS community. Ignoring the roll of the AIDS activists in the medical marijuana issue is inexcusable.)

Doctors are somewhat divided. Supporters of medical marijuana say it fights the nausea caused by chemotherapy and by AIDS treatments, allowing some patients to keep their strength at a crucial level.
See
Debate About Medical Marijuana Among Oregon Doctors
Tells Us More About Doctors Than About Marijuana. and links

Marijuana is alsosaidto relax the cramped and spasmodic muscles that torment some multiple sclerosis patients.

(Marijuananews note: He began his article with a story about an MS patient.)

But opponents say the evidence is far from conclusive. The Food and Drug Administration has not approved marijuana as safe and effective, and the Drug Enforcement Administration lists it as a "Schedule I" drug, meaning it has no medicinal value.
(Marijuananews note: This is the whole point of the initiatives.)

Barry McCaffrey, the nation’s drug czar, held a news conference Tuesday to drive home that point and to blast the state proposals.

That, however, is not the view of Stormy Ray, a multiple sclerosis patient in Oregon. She began smoking marijuana in 1991, she said, when her regular medicines stopped working.

"I was absolutely amazed," said Ray, a grandmother who said she had opposed drugs. "It was like somebody finally found the right way to turn my body back on. It took away the nerve pain. I could not imagine anything being able to do that."

If the initiatives do pass, that could be just the beginning of a tangled legal battle. The sale and possession of marijuana still would violate federal law, which takes precedence over state law.

In California, which passed a medical marijuana measure in 1996, legal confusion prevails. Federal authorities say they will crack down on doctors who recommended marijuana to their patients, but a court has put a temporary hold on that crackdown, and the final outcome is in doubt.
